title: A predictive theory of interacting endocrine control systems

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a quantitative theory that predicts how several interacting hormone systems respond to changes in the body or to interventions. It would connect hormone secretion, clearance, effective hormone responsiveness, gland growth and physiological state, explaining both the behavior of individual endocrine axes and the consequences of their interactions. Its defining advance would be reliable prediction of previously untested disturbances across systems and settings.

Hormone concentrations alone do not uniquely reveal the mechanisms maintaining them. Different combinations of production and removal can produce similar steady concentrations while generating different responses over time. A useful theory would distinguish these hidden mechanisms and predict their consequences. Effective hormone responsiveness is the appropriate interpretation of sensitivity here; the supplied study does not provide a comprehensive account of receptor biology. Differences in treatment response are a plausible inference from these mechanistic differences, rather than a clinical result established by that study.

The theory would need to connect processes operating at different speeds. The reviewed framework describes rapid hormone responses governed by removal rates over minutes to hours, alongside slower adaptation through changes in gland mass over weeks. It would also need to represent interactions between axes: for example, the study discusses cortisol's effects on thyroid, growth and gonadal regulation, including connections between the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal and hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid circuits.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would give endocrinology a transferable framework for predicting regulation across glands. Principles established in one system could generate quantitative, testable expectations in another, helping researchers choose informative perturbations and interpret apparently similar hormone measurements. The revolutionary step would be successful transfer to new conditions, beyond explaining observations already used to construct a model.

A plausible downstream application is better treatment design: predicting how changing one hormone, gland or tissue response affects the wider endocrine network, including adaptation after the initial response. Such predictions could help prioritize experiments and candidate interventions. The supplied paper discusses existing uses of endocrine models in clinical research, but it does not establish clinical usefulness or improved patient outcomes for the proposed general theory. Those benefits would require prospective clinical validation.

The analogy to a general control theory has limits. Shared feedback structures can suggest common behavior without making different endocrine systems biologically interchangeable. The documented five-class framework mainly considers textbook-defined circuits separately and uses schematic models. Its explanatory economy is valuable, but classification alone does not establish that a small set of rules can accurately predict coupled human physiology across all relevant conditions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is empirical generalization: turning shared circuit motifs into a theory that quantitatively predicts new responses across interacting endocrine systems. The reviewed work establishes mathematical functions of circuit classes, while leaving comparison with data from humans and other organisms, and more complete treatment of higher-level coupling, for further work. Models of isolated axes are an important foundation, but coupled-axis prediction is essential to this concept's scope.

One scientific barrier is identifying the underlying mechanisms from available measurements. Production, removal, gland mass and effective hormone responsiveness can have overlapping effects on observed concentrations. Because removal rates also affect response times, matching a baseline hormone level does not establish that a model will predict a disturbance correctly. A predictive account must distinguish parameter combinations sufficiently well to make useful dynamic predictions, including under physiological adaptation such as pregnancy, insulin resistance or chronic stress.

A second barrier is choosing the right level of biological detail. The reviewed models deliberately use a minimal set of production, removal and growth parameters, and the authors clarified that their models are schematic rather than definitive. Extending this approach requires determining which omitted mechanisms matter for each prediction, how slow gland adaptation interacts with faster hormone dynamics, and when interactions between axes change conclusions drawn from individual circuits.

Engineering synthesis: a usable implementation would need measurement and inference methods that estimate the quantities required for prediction, propagate uncertainty and identify conditions outside its demonstrated range. It would also need a disciplined way to connect models across timescales without adding so many adjustable parameters that agreement with existing data ceases to provide a meaningful test.

current_state.text: Moriya Raz and colleagues published “Unifying regulatory motifs in endocrine circuits” in Nature Communications on 21 November 2025. They found sufficient literature information for 43 of 63 human hormone systems and represented those 43 systems as 30 circuits falling into five circuit classes. The remaining 20 systems were excluded because information was insufficient. Thus, the classification covers the systems included in the analysis; it does not establish biological completeness across all endocrine regulation.

The study analyzed the dynamic functions of these classes using mathematical models, simulations and analytical solutions. It connects fast responses to hormone removal rates and emphasizes slower adaptation through gland-mass regulation. This is substantive progress toward general regulatory principles. It does not demonstrate a broadly predictive theory of coupled human endocrine systems, and the paper explicitly identifies comparison of modeling predictions with data from humans and other organisms as further work.

In the accompanying peer-review exchange, the authors clarified that their models were intended as schematic accounts rather than definitive models. That clarification helps delimit the achievement: shared motifs and their mathematical behavior provide hypotheses for biological testing. The exchange does not, by itself, negate the final paper's restrained claims or establish that its results are false.

The supplied review had full main-article text from retained HTML and the main-paper PDF, but did not visually inspect figures. Supplementary circuit diagrams were not recoverable from the supplied extraction, and one supplementary PDF had no substantive extracted text. These limitations constrain assessment of diagram-specific details; they do not prevent the textual assessment of the study's scope and numerical coverage given here.

Evidence limitation: the supplied material establishes this dated 2025 contribution, but contains no bounded search for subsequent developments. It therefore cannot establish the field-wide state as of 1 November 2026 or determine whether later work has achieved broader prospective prediction.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: the theory should produce quantitative, falsifiable predictions across several specified endocrine systems, including their interactions. Before testing, investigators should preregister predictions for withheld perturbations, including disturbances spanning coupled axes, and specify the species, human physiological settings and timescales covered. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not standards established by the reviewed paper.
completion_criteria.label: Preregister quantitative predictions for withheld perturbations across coupled endocrine axes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed comparative test: independent teams should prospectively confirm the predictions on genuinely new cases and compare them with appropriate system-specific models. Accuracy measures, uncertainty-calibration criteria and rules for declaring meaningful improvement should be specified in advance. The comparison should expose whether the general framework adds predictive value across systems and whether its stated uncertainty matches observed errors.
completion_criteria.label: Independent prospective tests confirm predictive gains and calibrated uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: investigators should make model definitions, parameter-estimation procedures and suitable validation data available for independent reproduction. Demonstrations should report where prediction succeeds, where it fails, and what measurements are needed to apply it. Finite tests would establish breadth within the tested systems and conditions, not literal universality. Use in treatment decisions would require additional clinical validation appropriate to the intended application.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction with reported predictive limits and measurement requirements

related_concepts.text: Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: END-03, an inexpensive continuous monitor for multiple human hormones, could supply richer time-series measurements for identifying and testing endocrine models. END-04 concerns the explanatory and predictive rules inferred from measurements; END-03 concerns acquiring those measurements. Better monitoring would not by itself resolve ambiguity between biological mechanisms.

Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: END-01, immune-protected renewable human islets, and END-02, a general platform for feedback-responsive endocrine replacement tissue, concern restoring physical hormone-producing systems. END-04 could help predict their integration with existing feedback and adaptation. It would not itself provide replacement tissue, immune protection or a transplantation method.

Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: END-07, regeneration of a person's own functional pancreatic beta cells, and END-08, restoration of ovarian endocrine function without previously banked tissue, focus on rebuilding particular sources of endocrine function. Their relevance to END-04 is the need to predict how restored secretion interacts with the wider hormonal network. Regeneration and restoration remain distinct biological achievements from a general predictive theory.

Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: END-05, durable resetting of dysfunctional energy-balance regulation, END-06, programmable tissue-selective control of hormone action, and END-09, glucose-responsive insulin, each seek an intervention that changes regulation or automates part of it. END-04 could help analyze adaptation, effective responsiveness and effects elsewhere in the network. Predicting an intervention's behavior would not establish that the intervention is feasible, durable or safe.

Conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster: END-10, durable antigen-specific tolerance in autoimmune endocrine disease, addresses immune mechanisms that can damage endocrine tissue. END-04 addresses endocrine regulation and its response to perturbations. It could describe consequences of preserving or losing gland function, but would not itself induce immune tolerance.

Methodologically, END-04 belongs to systems endocrinology and overlaps with control theory, systems biology and model identification. Its distinctive ambition is transfer across interacting glands, physiological states and timescales. The five-class circuit framework is a foundation for that ambition, while empirical validation of broader coupled-system predictions remains a separate step.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether later work achieved broader prospective prediction by 1 November 2026; no bounded freshness search was supplied.
The species, human physiological settings, coupled-axis perturbations, timescales and quantitative performance thresholds for a convincing demonstration remain to be specified.
The measurements needed to distinguish secretion, clearance, effective responsiveness and gland adaptation sufficiently for reliable prediction remain an open practical question.
The extent to which the five circuit classes generalize to the 20 systems excluded for insufficient information is unresolved.
Figure-specific and supplementary circuit details cannot be fully assessed from the supplied review because figures were not visually inspected and supplementary extraction was incomplete.
Prospective clinical usefulness and improved patient outcomes are not established by the supplied study.

brief.title: Reliable forecasts of the body's hormone responses
possible: Researchers could predict how changing a hormone, a gland or the body's response to hormones would affect other hormone systems. The forecasts would cover both the initial response and slower changes as glands grow or shrink. Hormones are the body's chemical signals.
why: Similar hormone measurements can hide different rates of production and removal. A predictive theory would help researchers distinguish those mechanisms and choose experiments that reveal how the systems work together.

Researchers could carry principles learned in one hormone system into another. This could help them choose candidate treatments by anticipating effects across the wider network, including adaptation after the initial response.

sources.showed: They grouped human hormone systems into shared patterns of control. Mathematical models linked those patterns to functions such as maintaining stable conditions and responding to changes.
sources.quote: We find that diverse systems can be organized into 5 classes of circuits according to shared regulatory motifs—regardless of biochemical detail.
sources.cited_for: Shared patterns of hormone control offer a foundation for a broader predictive theory.
sources.not_established: The models do not establish reliable predictions of new disturbances across interacting hormone systems.

sources.showed: They built a model connecting hormone pathways involved in stress. After adjustment for each person, it broadly matched exercise-response data from male firefighters.
sources.quote: After subject-specific parameter estimation, the proposed model that includes both the HPA and SA axes shows qualitative agreement with the collected data.
sources.cited_for: Connected stress pathways can be modeled together and fitted to individual hormone measurements.
sources.not_established: Matching fitted data does not establish prediction of new cases or transfer beyond exercise stress in male firefighters.

sources.showed: They built a model of the thyroid, a hormone-producing gland, and its control system. It reproduced measurements from experiments that administered hormones to volunteers with normal thyroid function.
sources.quote:
The ability of the model to reproduce
observed data is shown for different experimental conditions.
sources.cited_for: A detailed model of an individual hormone system can reproduce responses to administered hormones.
sources.not_established: The model does not establish prediction across interacting systems, thyroid diseases or conditions such as pregnancy.

sources.showed: They showed that a constant brain hormone signal could drive repeated pulses of stress hormones through interactions between glands.
sources.quote: We characterize a peripheral hormonal system and show that constant levels of corticotrophin-releasing hormone can induce and regulate hormone oscillations independent of the brain.
sources.cited_for: Mathematical predictions about the source of stress-hormone pulses received experimental support.
sources.not_established: A successful prediction within a stress-hormone pathway does not establish a theory that transfers across interacting hormone systems.

shown: Moriya Raz and colleagues organized the hormone systems they could characterize into five classes of control patterns and analyzed their behavior mathematically. Their models are deliberately simplified accounts of how these systems work.

Other teams have reproduced thyroid responses, fitted connected stress pathways to individual measurements, and experimentally supported predictions about stress-hormone pulses. These are foundations for broader prediction.
missing: A general theory has yet to reliably predict previously untested disturbances across interacting hormone systems.
Measurements must distinguish hormone production, removal, tissue responsiveness and gland growth well enough to support reliable forecasts.
Independent tests must establish whether the general theory predicts better than models built for individual systems.
Use in treatment decisions still requires clinical validation.

milestones.label: Predictions committed before tests across interacting hormone systems
milestones.explanation: Researchers would have to register numerical predictions before testing disturbances withheld from model development, with settings and timescales specified. This would test prediction across interacting systems.

milestones.label: Independent tests confirm better predictions and honest uncertainty
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to confirm gains over system-specific models on new cases using advance criteria, with stated uncertainty matching observed errors. This would establish added predictive value.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction establishes limits and required measurements
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce results using shared models, estimation methods and suitable data, reporting failures and required measurements. This would establish where the theory can be used reliably.

uncertain: The systems, physiological settings, timescales and accuracy needed for a convincing demonstration remain to be defined.
It remains unclear which biological details simplified models must retain to predict interactions and slow gland adaptation.
The shared control patterns may not extend to hormone systems excluded because too little is known about them.

page.title: Predictive models of interacting endocrine axes
page.definition: A quantitative framework predicts how interacting endocrine axes—chains of glands linked by hormones—respond to previously untested disturbances. It connects hormone secretion, removal and tissue responsiveness with slower changes in gland mass, and transfers between physiological states.

goal.need: Hormone secretion changes over minutes to hours, while endocrine gland mass adapts over weeks. Predicting responses therefore requires connecting these timescales. The 2025 circuit classification identified empirical testing and interactions between textbook-defined circuits as further work.

figures.caption: Coverage of the classification published on 21 November 2025
figures.note: These counts describe information available for circuit classification, not experimentally validated predictive models.

statements.quote: The Physiome Project aims to provide a quantitative modeling framework for understanding whole body function
statements.context: The Physiome Project concerns integrated physiology generally; it does not specify a completion test for endocrine modelling.

statements.context: The abstract of funded award OT2OD042764 describes a proposed female endocrine–metabolic modelling platform. Its performance period began on 14 September 2026.

completion.title: A shared endocrine model predicts new coupled-axis responses across physiological states.
completion.criterion: A shared mechanistic framework quantitatively predicts hormone responses to previously untested perturbations of interacting human endocrine axes, transferring between coupled-axis systems and physiological states. Test responses are excluded from model construction and parameter fitting. Predictions cover acute hormone dynamics and slower gland-mass adaptation, and receive independent experimental confirmation. Achievement is limited to the tested systems and states. No external accuracy tolerance, sample size or coverage count was found.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional criterion; no externally defined completion test was located for this capability.
completion.basis: Searches of Endocrine Society material, NIH programmes and awards, Physiome guidance, benchmarks, prizes and trial registries found no completion test for a general coupled-axis theory. Physiome guidance distinguishes fitting development data from predicting unused data but sets no error tolerance. This provisional Atlas test applies that distinction to transfer between systems, physiological states and timescales.

milestones.title: A rat endocrine model predicts sustained hormone oscillations under constant CRH infusion at 0.5 µg/h.
milestones.criterion: Experimental perturbation confirms a model prediction of sustained hormone oscillations under constant upstream stimulation. Walker et al., published on 5 June 2012, infused corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH) at 0.5 µg/h for 160 min in six rats. Samples every 20 min showed oscillations of pituitary adrenocorticotrophic hormone and adrenal corticosterone throughout infusion. This established a mechanism within one axis; it did not test coupling between axes.
milestones.set_by: Experimental confirmation of mechanistic predictions, a convention illustrated by Walker et al. and reviewed by Zavala et al. The numerical conditions belong to the published rat pituitary–adrenal experiment, not a general endocrine standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: constant infusion of CRH (0.5 µg/h) induced ultradian corticosterone oscillations that persisted throughout the infusion period

milestones.title: A model connecting human endocrine pathways reproduces measured hormone time courses.
milestones.criterion: Model solutions reproduce observed hormone time courses, satisfying the descriptive kinetic-model test in Physiome guidance; that guidance specifies no numerical fit tolerance. On 24 March 2026, Harris et al. reported individually estimated fits to 11 datasets from male firefighters cycling for 37 min at 60% of maximum oxygen consumption. Their connected hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal and sympathoadrenal model fitted cortisol, epinephrine and norepinephrine data. The authors reported qualitative agreement after fitting.
milestones.set_by: Physiome guidance hosted by NIH's Interagency Modeling and Analysis Group, introductory definition of Class 3 models. The definition applies to physiological models generally and is not a regulatory standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: kinetic descriptions of relationships between variables developed enough that model solutions fit observed time course behavior

milestones.title: A coupled endocrine model predicts hormone time courses in data excluded from its construction.
milestones.criterion: A model of interacting endocrine axes reproduces experimental hormone time courses excluded from its construction and parameter estimation. This applies the Physiome checklist's unused-data validation test to the coupled model, before broader transfer between systems and physiological states. The checklist specifies no numerical error tolerance, sample size or prospective-study requirement. The fitted two-pathway study does not establish this result because its evaluated data were used for parameter estimation.
milestones.set_by: Physiome model-validation practice represented by Bassingthwaighte's proposed 2010 checklist, Table 2, Group 4, item 3. The criterion appears in a table only, applies to physiological models generally, and was presented as proposed guidance.

not_found: No externally published completion test or numerical prediction-error threshold was found for a general theory of interacting endocrine axes.
No endocrine-specific consensus progression from laboratory demonstration to validated transfer between coupled systems was found.
The supplied thyroid-model PDF and its ScienceDirect article page returned HTTP 403 errors.
No qualifying independent test covering coupled-axis prediction and gland-mass adaptation across physiological states was identified in the sources checked.

results.finding: A coupled HPA–SA model achieved reasonable hormone fits for 11 firefighter datasets.
results.detail: Subject-specific parameters were estimated from cortisol, epinephrine and norepinephrine time-series data; the reported agreement was qualitative.
results.quote: While five representative datasets were shown, reasonable fits for B, E, and N were achieved for eleven datasets by performing Morris screening to determine the influential parameter set and using nonlinear optimization to estimate influential parameters based on available data.

results.finding: A coupled HPA–SA model fitted hormone time courses in 11 firefighter datasets.
results.detail: The evaluated data were used for parameter estimation; the source does not demonstrate prediction against data excluded from model construction and fitting.
results.quote: While five representative datasets were shown, reasonable fits for B, E, and N were achieved for eleven datasets by performing Morris screening to determine the influential parameter set and using nonlinear optimization to estimate influential parameters based on available data.

results.finding: A thyroid model reproduced fitted hormone time courses averaged over 33 subjects.
results.detail: The model represents the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis, rather than interactions between distinct endocrine axes.
results.quote:
Figs. 5 and 6 show the prediction ability of the proposed model for
T3, T4 and TSH plasma concentrations following the administration of
different doses of L-T4, referred to average observed time-courses on 33
subjects.

results.finding: A thyroid model was evaluated against fitted hormone time courses from 33 subjects.
results.detail: The model covers one endocrine axis, and the evaluated data were used for parameter estimation. The authors report that they could not split the data for independent validation.
results.quote:
The optimization procedure was performed simultaneously on
all observed variables, independently of the different LT4 dosages.

results.finding: In six rats, constant CRH infusion at 0.5 µg/h produced sustained ACTH and corticosterone oscillations, as predicted.
results.detail: Both hormones were sampled every 20 minutes during the 160-minute infusion. The experiment tested a mechanism within the pituitary–adrenal axis.
results.quote: In agreement with the modelling predictions, CRH induced ACTH and corticosterone oscillations that persisted throughout the infusion period
